items.title: Salient Features of the Indian Constitution
items.body:
## In one line

The salient features are the defining characteristics of the Constitution — written and lengthy, federal yet unitary, and parliamentary.

## Why it is asked

'Which is or is not a feature' and the current Article, Part and Schedule counts recur every year.

## Core features

- **Lengthiest written constitution** in the world — originally 395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules (1949); now about **470 Articles, 25 Parts, 12 Schedules**. Its bulk owes to the country's diversity, the influence of the **Government of India Act, 1935**, a single constitution for centre and states, and the role of legal experts.
- **Drawn from various sources** but tailored to Indian conditions (see the borrowed-sources note).
- **Blend of rigidity and flexibility** — Article 368 provides amendment by **special majority** and by **special majority + ratification by half the states**, while some provisions change by **simple majority**.
- **Federal system with unitary bias** — K.C. Wheare called it a **'quasi-federation'**. Article 1 calls India a **'Union of States'**: the federation is not an agreement of states and **no state can secede**. The word 'Federation' is never used.
- **Parliamentary (Westminster) government** at the centre and states, chosen over the US presidential system; but the **Indian Parliament is not sovereign** (laws face judicial review).
- **Synthesis of parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy** — Article 21 uses **'procedure established by law'** (not 'due process'); Parliament amends the Constitution, the Supreme Court exercises judicial review.
- **Single citizenship** despite a dual polity — one Indian citizenship for all (British model), unlike the US dual citizenship.
- **Universal adult franchise** (Art 326); voting age lowered from 21 to **18 by the 61st Amendment, 1988**.
- **Integrated and independent judiciary** — a single integrated system of courts, headed by the **Supreme Court**, with High Courts and subordinate courts below it, enforces **both central and state laws** (unlike the separate federal and state courts of the USA).
- **Independent bodies** set up by the Constitution itself to safeguard democracy: the **Election Commission of India**, the **Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG)**, the **Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)** and the State Public Service Commissions (SPSC). **Don't confuse:** **NITI Aayog** is NOT one of them — it was created by a Cabinet resolution (2015), not by the Constitution.
- A **three-tier government** (Union, State, local) — local government added by the **73rd/74th Amendments, 1992**.
- **A secular state** — positive secularism: the state gives **equal respect and protection to all religions** without endorsing any one as the official faith. This differs from the Western model of complete separation of religion and state.

## Terms explained

- **Quasi-federation** — federal in form but with a strong tilt towards the Centre (K.C. Wheare’s term).
- **‘Procedure established by law’** — a person’s liberty can be taken only by a set legal procedure (narrower than the American ‘due process’).
- **Universal adult franchise** — every adult citizen’s right to vote, regardless of wealth or education.
- **Single citizenship** — one national citizenship for all Indians, unlike the dual citizenship of the United States.

## TL;DR

- Lengthiest written constitution: original 395 Articles/22 Parts/8 Schedules (1949); now about 470/25/12.
- Blend of rigidity and flexibility via Article 368: simple, special, and special-plus-state-ratification amendments.
- Quasi-federal (K.C. Wheare); Article 1 = 'Union of States' — no secession, not an agreement of states; word 'Federation' never used.
- Parliamentary (Westminster) system adopted; Indian Parliament is NOT sovereign (unlike Britain).
- Single citizenship (British model) despite a dual polity; universal adult franchise under Art 326, age 18 via 61st Amendment (1988).

Single citizenship (British model) despite a dual polity; universal adult franchise under Art 326, age 18 via 61st Amendment (1988).
Constitutional independent bodies: Election Commission, CAG, UPSC and SPSCs; NITI Aayog (2015) is not a constitutional body.

items.title: Sources Borrowed from Other Constitutions
items.body:
## In one line

A ready-reference of which feature of the Constitution was borrowed from which country.

## Why it is asked

Source-matching is among the most repeated objective questions.

## Country-to-feature map

| Source | Features borrowed |
|---|---|
| **British** | Parliamentary government, rule of law, bicameralism, cabinet system, single citizenship, prerogative writs |
| **US** | Fundamental Rights, independence of judiciary, judicial review, impeachment of President, removal of judges, VP's post |
| **Irish** | Directive Principles of State Policy, method of President's election, nomination of Rajya Sabha members |
| **Soviet (USSR)** | Fundamental Duties, ideal of justice (social, economic, political) in the Preamble |
| **Canadian** | Strong-centre federation, residuary powers with the centre, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction of SC |
| **Australian** | Concurrent List, joint sitting of Parliament, freedom of trade and commerce |
| **Weimar (Germany)** | Emergency provisions for suspension of Fundamental Rights |
| **French** | Republic; ideals of Liberty, Equality, Fraternity |
| **Japanese** | Procedure established by law (Art 21) |
| **GoI Act, 1935** | Federal scheme, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, office of Governor, emergency provisions |
| **South African** | Amendment procedure, election of Rajya Sabha members |

- Borrowed features were **adapted** to Indian conditions — for example, the cabinet system does not carry the same supremacy as in the UK.

## Terms explained

- **Writs** — formal court orders (such as Habeas Corpus) used to protect rights, borrowed from Britain.
- **DPSP (Directive Principles of State Policy)** — guidelines the State should follow, borrowed from Ireland.
- **Concurrent List** — subjects on which both the Centre and the states may legislate, borrowed from Australia.

## Don't confuse

- **DPSP (Ireland) vs Fundamental Duties (USSR)** — the Directive Principles come from Ireland; the Fundamental Duties come from the Soviet (USSR) constitution.
- **Emergency provisions** — the *suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency* is from **Weimar Germany**, while the broader *federal and emergency scheme* is from the **GoI Act, 1935**.
- **Canada vs US federalism** — a strong-centre federation with residuary powers at the Centre is **Canadian**; the US model is a weaker-centre federation with residuary powers in the states.
- **Procedure established by law (Japan)** vs the American *due process of law* — the Indian text borrows the Japanese wording.

## Remember it

- 'Duties are Soviet, Principles are Irish; Emergency-FR-suspension is German, the skeleton is 1935.'

## TL;DR

- British: parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, writs.
- US: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, VP's post.
- Irish: Directive Principles of State Policy; Soviet/USSR: Fundamental Duties.
- Canadian: strong-centre federation and residuary powers; Australian: Concurrent List and joint sitting.
- Weimar (Germany): suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency; GoI Act 1935: federal scheme and emergency provisions.
keyPoints: British: parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, writs.
US: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, VP's post.
Irish: Directive Principles of State Policy; Soviet/USSR: Fundamental Duties.
Canadian: strong-centre federation and residuary powers; Australian: Concurrent List and joint sitting.
Weimar (Germany): suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency; GoI Act 1935: federal scheme and emergency provisions.
items.mnemonic: DPSP = Ireland's gift; Duties = the USSR's; Emergency FR-suspension = Germany's Weimar.

items.title: The Preamble — Text, Components & 42nd Amendment
items.body:
## In one line

The Preamble is the short opening statement of the Constitution that declares its ideals and the source of its authority (the people of India).

## Why it is asked

Its exact words, the 42nd Amendment additions and the link to the Objectives Resolution are standard questions.

## What the Preamble is

- The **introductory statement** to the Constitution, outlining its **guiding principles and philosophy**. It is based on the **Objectives Resolution** moved by **Jawaharlal Nehru** and adopted by the Constituent Assembly.

## Four components

1. **Source of authority** — 'WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA'; the Constitution derives its authority from the people.
2. **Nature of the state** — Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
3. **Objectives** — Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.
4. **Date of adoption** — 26 November 1949.

## The 42nd Amendment (1976)

- The Preamble has been amended **only once** — the 42nd Amendment added **'Socialist'** and **'Secular'** to the state's description and **'and integrity'** to 'unity of the nation'.

## Keyword sources

| Term | Borrowed from |
|---|---|
| We, the people of India | USA |
| Justice | Russian Revolution / USA |
| Liberty | French Revolution / USA |
| Equality, Fraternity | French Revolution |

- Scholars' praise: **K.M. Munshi** — 'horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'; **Thakur Das Bhargava** — 'soul of the Constitution'; **Ernest Barker** — 'key-note to the Constitution'.

## Terms explained

- **Preamble** — the short opening declaration that states the ideals of the Constitution and that its authority comes from the people.
- **Objectives Resolution** — Nehru’s statement of aims on which the Preamble is based.
- **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic** — independent of outside control; aiming at social-economic equality; equal respect for all religions; ruled by elected representatives; with an elected (not hereditary) head of state.

## TL;DR

- Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru.
- Four components: source of authority (We the People), nature of state, objectives, date (26 Nov 1949).
- Keywords describing the state: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic.
- Objectives: Justice (social/economic/political), Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.
- Amended only once — 42nd Amendment (1976) added Socialist, Secular and Integrity.

items.title: Status of the Preamble — Key Cases
items.body:
## In one line

This traces, through court cases, whether the Preamble is actually part of the Constitution and whether it can be amended.

## Why it is asked

The Berubari to Kesavananda to LIC case ladder is tested often.

## Is the Preamble a part of the Constitution?

| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **Berubari Union** | 1960 | Preamble is the 'key to open the mind of the makers' but **NOT a part** of the Constitution; not enforceable. |
| **Kesavananda Bharati** | 1973 | Preamble **IS a part** of the Constitution and can be amended (subject to the basic structure). |
| **Union Govt v. LIC of India** | 1995 | Reaffirmed the Preamble is **an integral part**, but is **not directly enforceable** in a court. |

## Takeaways

- The Preamble **can be amended** under Article 368, but its **basic features cannot be destroyed**.
- It is **not a source of power** nor a limitation on powers, and it is **non-justiciable** (not enforceable by courts).

## Don't confuse

'**Part of the Constitution**' and '**enforceable**' are not the same thing. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that the Preamble **is a part** of the Constitution, but no court enforces the Preamble by itself — it only helps interpret other provisions.

## Terms explained

- **Justiciable / non-justiciable** — enforceable in a court versus not enforceable by itself.
- **Basic structure** — the Constitution’s core features that even an amendment cannot destroy.
- **‘Part of the Constitution’ vs ‘enforceable’** — being a part means it can guide interpretation; being enforceable would mean a court could act on it directly. The Preamble is a part but not enforceable on its own.

## TL;DR

- Berubari (1960): Preamble is NOT part of the Constitution and not enforceable.
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Preamble IS part of the Constitution and is amendable.
- LIC of India (1995): Preamble is an integral part but not directly enforceable.
- The Preamble can be amended under Art 368 but its basic features cannot be destroyed.
- The Preamble is non-justiciable — not enforceable in a court of law.

items.title: Parts of the Constitution — Quick Reference
items.body:
## In one line

A quick map of the Constitution's Parts and which Articles each Part covers.

## Why it is asked

'Which Part deals with X' is a reliable one-mark question.

## Key Parts and their Articles

| Part | Subject | Articles |
|---|---|---|
| I | The Union and its Territory | 1-4 |
| II | Citizenship | 5-11 |
| III | Fundamental Rights | 12-35 |
| IV | Directive Principles (DPSP) | 36-51 |
| IVA | Fundamental Duties | 51A |
| V | The Union (Executive/Legislature/Judiciary) | 52-151 |
| VI | The States | 152-237 |
| IX | The Panchayats | 243-243O |
| IXA | The Municipalities | 243P-243ZG |
| IXB | Co-operative Societies | 243ZH-243ZT |
| XI | Union-State Relations | 245-263 |
| XIVA | Tribunals | 323A-323B |
| XVIII | Emergency Provisions | 352-360 |
| XX | Amendment of the Constitution | 368 |

- **Parts added later**: IXA & IXB (73rd/74th & 97th Amendments), XIVA (42nd Amendment). Part VII was **repealed** by the 7th Amendment.
- The document was **handwritten** (Hindi and English), drafted in **2 years, 11 months, 18 days**, adopted **26 Nov 1949**, enforced **26 Jan 1950**.

## Terms explained

- **Part** — a numbered division of the Constitution that groups related Articles together.
- **Article** — a single numbered provision of the Constitution.
- **Repealed** — formally removed or cancelled (as Part VII was by the 7th Amendment).

## TL;DR

- Part III = Fundamental Rights (12-35); Part IV = DPSP (36-51); Part IVA = Fundamental Duties (51A).
- Part IX = Panchayats, IXA = Municipalities, IXB = Co-operative Societies.
- Part XIVA = Tribunals (added by 42nd Amendment); Part VII repealed by 7th Amendment.
- Part XVIII = Emergency Provisions (352-360); Part XX = Amendment (Art 368).
- Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950; drafted in 2 years 11 months 18 days.

items.title: Schedules of the Constitution — Quick Reference
items.body:
## In one line

A quick map of the twelve Schedules and the subject each one lists.

## Why it is asked

Schedule-matching (anti-defection, official languages, panchayats) is a repeat favourite.

## The 12 Schedules

| Schedule | Subject |
|---|---|
| First | States and Union Territories |
| Second | Salaries of officials (President, Governors, Judges, etc.) |
| Third | Forms of oaths and affirmations |
| Fourth | Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha |
| Fifth | Administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes |
| Sixth | Administration of Tribal Areas (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) |
| **Seventh** | Union, State and Concurrent Lists (division of powers) |
| **Eighth** | 22 official languages |
| **Ninth** | Land reform laws (protected under Art 31-B) |
| **Tenth** | Anti-Defection Law |
| **Eleventh** | Powers of Panchayats (Art 243-G) |
| **Twelfth** | Powers of Municipalities (Art 243-W) |

## Amendment origins

- **9th Schedule** — added by the **1st Amendment, 1951** (shield land-reform laws from judicial review).
- **10th Schedule** — added by the **52nd Amendment, 1985** (Anti-Defection).
- **11th & 12th Schedules** — added by the **73rd & 74th Amendments, 1992**.
- The Constitution began with **8 Schedules**; the concept was first seen in the **GoI Act, 1935** (10 schedules).

## Terms explained

- **Schedule** — an appendix at the end of the Constitution that lists details such as languages, salaries or the three legislative lists.
- **Anti-Defection Law** — rules (Tenth Schedule) that disqualify a legislator who defects from the party on whose ticket they were elected.
- **Ninth Schedule** — a list of laws (mostly land reform) placed beyond ordinary court challenge.

## TL;DR

- 7th Schedule = Union/State/Concurrent Lists; 8th Schedule = 22 official languages.
- 9th Schedule = land reform laws (Art 31-B), added by 1st Amendment (1951).
- 10th Schedule = Anti-Defection Law, added by 52nd Amendment (1985).
- 11th (Panchayats) and 12th (Municipalities) Schedules added by 73rd/74th Amendments (1992).
- Original Constitution had 8 Schedules; now 12.
keyPoints: 7th Schedule = Union/State/Concurrent Lists; 8th Schedule = 22 official languages.
9th Schedule = land reform laws (Art 31-B), added by 1st Amendment (1951).
10th Schedule = Anti-Defection Law, added by 52nd Amendment (1985).
11th (Panchayats) and 12th (Municipalities) Schedules added by 73rd/74th Amendments (1992).
Original Constitution had 8 Schedules; now 12.
items.mnemonic: High-yield Schedules '7-8-9-10' = Lists, Languages, Land-reform, Loyalty (anti-defection).

items.title: Exam-Precision: Preamble Liberties, Welfare State & Limited Government
items.body:
## In one line

The precise Preamble wording and the idea of limited (constitutional) government that papers have asked exactly.

## Why it is asked

Distractors such as 'economic liberty' are deliberately planted here.

## Which 'Liberty' does the Preamble grant?

The Preamble secures **Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship**. It does **NOT** mention **'economic liberty'** - a favourite UPSC distractor. (Economic content enters through *Justice*, not *Liberty*.)

| Preamble word | Exact scope |
|---|---|
| **Justice** | social, **economic** and political |
| **Liberty** | thought, expression, belief, faith, worship |
| **Equality** | of status and of opportunity |
| **Fraternity** | dignity of the individual; unity and integrity of the nation |

## Where objectives are echoed elsewhere

- **Economic Justice** as an objective is provided in **both the Preamble AND the Directive Principles of State Policy** (Part IV, esp. Arts 38-39).
- The ideal of a **Welfare State** is enshrined in the **Directive Principles of State Policy** (not the Preamble or Fundamental Rights).
- **UDHR (1948)** ideals are reflected in the **Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties**.
- The Fundamental Duty to 'uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India' is in **Article 51A (Part IVA)**, not the Preamble.

## Constitutional (limited) government

- A **constitutional government** places **restrictions on the authority of the State in the interest of individual liberty** - that is, limited government. It is the opposite of restricting individual liberty in favour of State authority.
- **How India differs from Britain**: the British Parliament is **sovereign/supreme**, but the **Indian Parliament's power to legislate is limited** by a written Constitution and judicial review.

## Terms explained

- **Liberty in the Preamble** — freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; it does not include ‘economic liberty’.
- **Welfare state** — a state that promotes citizens’ well-being; this ideal sits in the Directive Principles, not the Preamble.
- **Constitutional (limited) government** — a government whose power over citizens is restricted in favour of individual liberty.
- **UDHR (1948)** — the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, whose ideals are reflected in the Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties.

## TL;DR

- Preamble grants Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship - NOT 'economic liberty'.
- Economic Justice as an objective is provided in both the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy.
- The ideal of a Welfare State is enshrined in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
- UDHR (1948) ideals are reflected in the Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties.
- A constitutional (limited) government restricts the State's authority in favour of individual liberty.
keyPoints: Preamble grants Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship - NOT 'economic liberty'.
Economic Justice as an objective is provided in both the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy.
The ideal of a Welfare State is enshrined in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
UDHR (1948) ideals are reflected in the Preamble, the DPSP and the Fundamental Duties.
A constitutional (limited) government restricts the State's authority in favour of individual liberty.
The British Parliament is sovereign, but the Indian Parliament's legislative power is limited by judicial review and a written Constitution.

items.title: Salient Features in Detail — Structure, Federalism, Parliament, Bodies & Criticism
items.body:
## The structural features, one by one

**In one line:** the Constitution is long, partly rigid and partly flexible, federal with a strong Centre, parliamentary, and backed by independent bodies — and each feature has its exam detail.

**Why it is asked:** "Which is NOT a federal feature?", "Which body is constitutional?", "Which Article for which emergency?" and "Who called the Constitution what?" are standard one-markers.

**The story**

### Size
- Constitutions are either **written** (like the USA's) or **unwritten** (like the UK's); India's is written.
- Originally (1949) a Preamble, **395 Articles in 22 Parts** and **8 Schedules**; the source counts **448 Articles in 25 Parts and 12 Schedules (as of October 2024)**. (Counting lettered Articles such as 21A, the total is about 470 — references differ.)
- It has been amended **106 times** as of 2024 (the 106th Amendment, 2023, reserved one-third of seats for women).
- Four reasons for its length: the country's **vastness and diversity**; the influence of the **Government of India Act 1935**; a **single constitution for the Centre and the states**; and the dominance of **legal experts** in the Assembly.

### Rigid and flexible (Article 368)
| Method | What it needs |
|---|---|
| **Special majority** | A majority of the **total membership** of each House **and** **two-thirds of members present and voting** |
| **Special majority + states** | The above **plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures** (federal provisions) |
| **Simple majority** | More than half of members **present and voting**, by the ordinary law-making process (outside Article 368) |

### Federal system with a unitary bias
- **Federal features:** two governments, **division of powers**, a **written** Constitution, **supremacy** of the Constitution, **rigidity**, an **independent judiciary** and **bicameralism**.
- **Unitary (non-federal) features:** a **strong Centre**, a **single constitution**, **single citizenship**, **flexibility**, an **integrated judiciary**, **appointment of Governors by the Centre**, **all-India services** and **emergency provisions**.
- **Article 1** calls India a **"Union of States"**: the federation is **not the result of an agreement** among the states, and **no state can secede**. The word **"Federation" is not used** anywhere in the Constitution.
- What scholars called it: **K.C. Wheare** – "**quasi-federal**"; **Granville Austin** – "**co-operative federalism**"; **Morris-Jones** – "**bargaining federalism**"; **Ivor Jennings** – "a federation with a strong **centralising tendency**".

### Parliamentary government
- Also called the **Westminster model**, **responsible government** and **cabinet government**; adopted at the Centre **and in the states**, in preference to the American presidential system.
- Features: **nominal and real executives**; **majority-party rule**; **collective responsibility** of the executive to the legislature; ministers are **members of the legislature**; leadership of the **Prime Minister / Chief Minister**; **dissolution** of the lower House.
- Two differences from Britain: the **Indian Parliament is not sovereign**, and India has an **elected head** of state (a **republic**), not a hereditary monarch.
- **Synthesis of parliamentary sovereignty (Britain) and judicial supremacy (USA):** the Supreme Court can strike down laws by **judicial review**, while Parliament can amend most of the Constitution by its **constituent power**. Article 21 uses the Japanese "**procedure established by law**", not the American "**due process of law**".

### Integrated and independent judiciary
- One hierarchy — **Supreme Court → High Courts → subordinate courts** — enforces **both central and state laws**.
- The Supreme Court is a **federal court**, the **highest court of appeal**, the **guarantor of Fundamental Rights** and the **guardian of the Constitution**. Independence is protected by **security of tenure** and **fixed service conditions** of judges.

### Independent bodies and emergencies
| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **Election Commission** | Free and fair elections |
| **Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG)** | Audits the accounts of the Centre and the states |
| **UPSC** | Recruits to all-India and higher central services; advises the **President** on disciplinary matters |
| **State PSC** | Recruits to state services; advises the **Governor** on disciplinary matters |

| Emergency | Ground | Article |
|---|---|---|
| **National Emergency** | War, external aggression or armed rebellion | **352** |
| **President's Rule (State Emergency)** | Failure of constitutional machinery in a state; failure to comply with Union directions | **356**, **365** |
| **Financial Emergency** | Threat to financial stability or credit of India | **360** |

### Other features
- **Secular state:** the word "**Secular**" entered the Preamble by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**. The **Western** idea is a complete separation of religion and state; the **Indian** idea is **positive** — equal respect and protection for all religions.
- **Universal adult franchise:** **Article 326**; every citizen aged **18** may vote for the Lok Sabha and state assemblies. The **61st Amendment Act, 1988** lowered the age from **21 to 18** (in force from **1989**).
- **Single citizenship** despite a **dual polity** — unlike the **USA**, where a person is a citizen of the country and of his state.
- India has **only one citizenship and one domicile**; a citizen by **naturalisation** can also become Head of State, and any citizen can be **deprived** of citizenship under law (UPSC 2021).
- The best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy is the **separation of powers** (UPSC 2021).
- A constitutional government places restrictions on the authority of the State in the interest of individual liberty (limited government; UPSC 2014).
- **Three-tier government:** the **73rd Amendment (1992)** gave panchayats constitutional status (**Part IX**, **Eleventh Schedule**); the **74th Amendment (1992)** did the same for municipalities (**Part IXA**, **Twelfth Schedule**) — a third tier "not found in any other constitution".

### Criticism and the reply
| Criticism | Critic | Counter |
|---|---|---|
| **Borrowed constitution** / "slavish imitation of the West" | **Lokanath Misra** | Borrowed features were **adapted** to Indian conditions |
| **Carbon copy of the 1935 Act** | Critics in the Assembly | Only the administrative framework was taken; many innovations were added |
| **Un-Indian / anti-Indian** | Critics | It reflects Indian ideals and aspirations |
| **Un-Gandhian** — "we wanted the music of the **veena** or the **sitar**, but here we have the music of an English band" | **K. Hanumanthaiya** | It still embodies Gandhian values (DPSP, panchayats, social justice) |
| **Elephantine size** | Critics (Ivor Jennings: too long, too rigid) | Size needed for India's diversity |
| **Paradise for lawyers** | **Ivor Jennings** | Legal language gives clarity and enforceability |

## Don't confuse
- **Special majority** (Article 368) ≠ **simple majority** (ordinary process).
- **Quasi-federal = Wheare**; **co-operative = Austin**; **bargaining = Morris-Jones**.
- **UPSC advises the President; State PSC advises the Governor.**

**TL;DR**
- 448 Articles / 25 Parts / 12 Schedules (2024); 106 amendments; length due to diversity, 1935 Act, single constitution, lawyers.
- Federal features: two governments, division of powers, written, supreme, rigid, independent judiciary, bicameral; unitary: strong Centre, single constitution, single citizenship, integrated judiciary, Governors, all-India services, emergency.
- Article 1 "Union of States": no agreement, no secession; "Federation" never used.
- Emergencies: 352 national, 356/365 President's Rule, 360 financial.
- Critics: Lokanath Misra (borrowed), Hanumanthaiya (veena/sitar), Ivor Jennings (lawyers' paradise).
keyPoints: Source count: 448 Articles, 25 Parts, 12 Schedules (October 2024); amended 106 times as of 2024.
Length due to vastness and diversity, the 1935 Act, a single constitution for Centre and states, and legal experts.
Special majority = majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting; some provisions also need ratification by half the states.
Unitary features: strong Centre, single constitution, single citizenship, integrated judiciary, Governors appointed by the Centre, all-India services, emergency provisions.
K.C. Wheare 'quasi-federal'; Granville Austin 'co-operative federalism'; Morris-Jones 'bargaining federalism'; Ivor Jennings 'strong centralising tendency'.
Parliamentary features: nominal and real executives, majority-party rule, collective responsibility, ministers in the legislature, PM/CM leadership, dissolution of the lower House.
Emergencies: Article 352 (national), 356 and 365 (President's Rule), 360 (financial); UPSC advises the President, State PSC the Governor.
Critics: Lokanath Misra (slavish imitation), K. Hanumanthaiya (veena or sitar vs English band), Ivor Jennings (lawyers' paradise).

items.title: Rights, Writs, Duties & Directives as Salient Features
items.body:
## Rights, remedies, duties and directives — the feature view

**In one line:** the Constitution guarantees six Fundamental Rights backed by five writs, adds eleven Fundamental Duties and lays down Directive Principles that courts cannot enforce.

**Why it is asked:** writ meanings ("we command", "by what authority") and the 97th Amendment's three changes for co-operatives are quick one-markers.

**The story**

### Six Fundamental Rights (Part III)
| Right | Articles | Core content |
|---|---|---|
| **Right to Equality** | **14–18** | Equality before law; no discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; **abolition of untouchability** |
| **Right to Freedom** | **19–22** | Speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession; protection against arbitrary **arrest and detention** |
| **Right against Exploitation** | **23–24** | Bans **human trafficking**, **forced labour** and **child labour** |
| **Right to Freedom of Religion** | **25–28** | Freedom of **conscience**; profess, practise and propagate religion |
| **Cultural and Educational Rights** | **29–30** | Minorities may preserve **language, script and culture** and set up educational institutions |
| **Right to Constitutional Remedies** | **32** | Move the **Supreme Court** to enforce Fundamental Rights |

### The five writs (from English law, enforced through Article 32)
| Writ | Meaning | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Habeas Corpus** | "**you may have the body**" | Produce a detained person before the court — no **unlawful detention** |
| **Mandamus** | "**we command**" | Direct an official or lower court to perform a **public or statutory duty** |
| **Prohibition** | "to forbid" | A higher court **stops** a lower court from **exceeding its jurisdiction** |
| **Certiorari** | "to be certified" | **Quash** an order of a lower court or authority made without jurisdiction or against natural justice |
| **Quo Warranto** | "**by what authority**" | Question a person's right to hold a **public office** |

### Fundamental Duties (Part IVA)
- **Part IVA** has only **Article 51A**, listing **eleven** duties. The original Constitution had **none**.
- Added during the **internal Emergency (1975–77)** by the **42nd Amendment Act 1976**, on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**; the **86th Amendment Act 2002** added the eleventh duty.
- They are **non-justiciable** — courts cannot enforce them directly.

### Directive Principles (Part IV)
- **B.R. Ambedkar** called the DPSP a "**novel feature**" of the Constitution.
- Three groups: **socialistic**, **Gandhian** and **liberal-intellectual**.
- **Non-justiciable**, yet **fundamental in the governance** of the country — the State must apply them in making laws.

### Co-operative societies — the 97th Amendment Act, 2011
1. Made the right to form **co-operative societies** a **Fundamental Right** under **Article 19**.
2. Added a new Directive Principle on their promotion — **Article 43B**.
3. Added **Part IXB, "The Co-operative Societies"** (**Articles 243ZH to 243ZT**).

## Don't confuse
- **Mandamus = "we command"**; **Quo Warranto = "by what authority"**; **Habeas Corpus = "you may have the body"**.
- **Prohibition** stops a case *before* the order; **Certiorari** quashes an order *already made*.
- FRs are **justiciable**; DPSP and Fundamental Duties are **non-justiciable**.

**TL;DR**
- FRs: 14–18, 19–22, 23–24, 25–28, 29–30, 32.
- Five writs from English law under Article 32: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto.
- Fundamental Duties: Part IVA, Article 51A, eleven; 42nd (1976, Swaran Singh) + 86th (2002).
- DPSP: Ambedkar's "novel feature"; socialistic, Gandhian, liberal-intellectual.
- 97th Amendment 2011: Article 19 right, Article 43B, Part IXB (243ZH–243ZT).
keyPoints: FR groups: Equality 14-18, Freedom 19-22, against Exploitation 23-24, Religion 25-28, Cultural and Educational 29-30, Constitutional Remedies 32.
Habeas Corpus 'you may have the body'; Mandamus 'we command'; Quo Warranto 'by what authority'; Prohibition stops excess of jurisdiction; Certiorari quashes an order.
Writs come from the legal system of England and are enforced through Article 32.
Part IVA (Article 51A) has eleven duties; added by the 42nd Amendment 1976 (Swaran Singh Committee); the 86th Amendment 2002 added the eleventh.
Ambedkar called the DPSP a 'novel feature'; three groups — socialistic, Gandhian, liberal-intellectual.
97th Amendment 2011: co-operatives a right under Article 19, new DPSP Article 43B, Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT).

items.title: The Preamble in Detail — Text, Keywords, Quotes & Court Rulings
items.body:
## The Preamble, word by word

**In one line:** the Preamble says who made the Constitution (the people), what kind of State India is, what it aims at, and when it was adopted — and the courts have ruled on whether it is part of the Constitution.

**Why it is asked:** exact phrases ("equality of status and of opportunity", "dignity of the individual"), the meaning of each keyword and the case ladder are tested every year.

- It is the introductory statement setting out the guiding principles and philosophy of the Constitution, with four components: the **source of authority**, the **nature of the State**, the **objectives** and the **date of adoption**.

**The story**

### The text (as amended in 1976)
> WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a **SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC** and to secure to all its citizens:
> **JUSTICE**, social, economic and political;
> **LIBERTY** of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;
> **EQUALITY** of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all
> **FRATERNITY** assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation;
> IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY **ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES** THIS CONSTITUTION.

### What each keyword means
| Keyword | Meaning in India |
|---|---|
| **Sovereign** | India is independent — no external authority above it, free in internal and external affairs |
| **Socialist** | **Democratic socialism** — a **mixed economy**, not state ownership of everything (added 1976) |
| **Secular** | All religions get **equal respect**; no official State religion (added 1976) |
| **Democratic** | **Representative parliamentary** democracy; political and social-economic democracy |
| **Republic** | The head of State (**President**) is **elected**, not hereditary |

### The 42nd Amendment and later rulings
- The Preamble has been amended **only once** — by the **42nd Amendment Act 1976**, which added **Socialist**, **Secular** and **Integrity** ("unity of the Nation" became "**unity and integrity of the Nation**").
- On **26 January 1950** India was therefore a **Sovereign Democratic Republic**.
- In **November 2024** (**Dr Balram Singh v. Union of India**) the Supreme Court **upheld** the insertion of "Socialist" and "Secular", rejecting the plea that the 1976 change was invalid because the adoption date in the text is 1949.
- **S.R. Bommai case (1994):** **secularism** is part of the **basic structure**.

### Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?
| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **Berubari Union** (a **Presidential reference under Article 143** on transferring Berubari to Pakistan) | **1960** | "**Key to open the mind of the makers**", but **not a part** of the Constitution |
| **Kesavananda Bharati** | **1973** | **Is a part** of the Constitution; can be **amended under Article 368**, but **not its basic features** |
| **LIC of India** | **1995** | An **integral part** of the Constitution, **not directly enforceable** |

- The Preamble is **neither a source of power** to the legislature **nor a limit** on its powers, and it is **non-justiciable**.

### Where the ideals came from
| Ideal | Source |
|---|---|
| "We, the people of India" (the idea of a Preamble) | **USA** |
| **Justice** — social, economic, political | **Russian Revolution (1917)** |
| **Liberty, Equality, Fraternity** | **French Revolution (1789)** |

### What people said about it
| Person | Description |
|---|---|
| **Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar** | It "expresses what we had thought or dreamt for so long" |
| **K.M. Munshi** | "**Horoscope** of our sovereign democratic republic" |
| **Thakur Das Bhargava** | "**Soul** of the Constitution", "a **jewel** set in the Constitution", "a proper **yardstick**" |
| **Ernest Barker** | "**Key-note** to the Constitution" |
| **M. Hidayatullah** | Resembles the American **Declaration of Independence** but is more; "the soul of our Constitution" |
| **N.A. Palkhivala** | "**Identity card** of the Constitution" |

## Don't confuse
- **Justice** has three types (social, economic, political); **Liberty** has five (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship); **Equality** has two (status, opportunity).
- **Horoscope = Munshi**; **identity card = Palkhivala**; **key-note = Barker**; **soul/jewel = Thakur Das Bhargava**.

**TL;DR**
- Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity; adopted 26 November 1949.
- Socialist = democratic socialism (mixed economy); Republic = elected head.
- Only one amendment: 42nd (1976) — Socialist, Secular, Integrity; upheld in Balram Singh (Nov 2024).
- Berubari 1960 (Article 143 reference): not part; Kesavananda 1973: part, amendable; LIC 1995: integral, not enforceable; Bommai 1994: secularism basic.
- Justice from the Russian Revolution; liberty-equality-fraternity from the French Revolution.
keyPoints: Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; Equality of status and of opportunity; Fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation.
The Preamble ends: 'do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION' (26 November 1949).
Socialist means democratic socialism (a mixed economy); Republic means an elected head of State.
Berubari (1960) was a Presidential reference under Article 143; S.R. Bommai (1994) made secularism part of the basic structure.
In November 2024 (Dr Balram Singh v. Union of India) the Supreme Court upheld the 42nd Amendment's insertion of Socialist and Secular.
The Preamble is neither a source of power nor a limitation on the legislature.
Quotes: Munshi 'horoscope'; Thakur Das Bhargava 'soul'; Barker 'key-note'; Palkhivala 'identity card'; Hidayatullah — like the US Declaration of Independence.

items.title: All 25 Parts & 12 Schedules — Complete Reference
items.body:
## Every Part and every Schedule

**In one line:** the Constitution is arranged in 25 Parts (Articles grouped by subject) and 12 Schedules (lists at the end); examiners ask which Part or Schedule holds which subject and which amendment added it.

**Why it is asked:** "Part XIII deals with?", "Which Schedule has Articles 102 and 191?" and "Which Part was repealed?" are recurring items; APPSC adds Article 371D (Andhra Pradesh).

**The story**

### The 25 Parts
| Part | Subject | Articles |
|---|---|---|
| Part I | The Union and its Territory ("**Union of States**") | 1–4 |
| Part II | Citizenship | 5–11 |
| Part III | Fundamental Rights (inspired by the **US Bill of Rights**) | 12–35 |
| Part IV | Directive Principles of State Policy | 36–51 |
| Part IVA | Fundamental Duties | 51A |
| Part V | The Union — Executive (**52–78**), Parliament (**79–122**), Supreme Court (**124–147**), CAG | 52–151 |
| Part VI | The States — Executive (**153–167**), Legislature (**168–212**), High Courts (**214–237**) | 152–237 |
| Part VII | States in Part B of the First Schedule — **repealed by the 7th Amendment (1956)** | — |
| Part VIII | The Union Territories (an **administrator** appointed by the President for each) | 239–242 |
| Part IX | The Panchayats (**73rd Amendment, 1992**) | 243–243O |
| Part IXA | The Municipalities (**74th Amendment, 1992**) | 243P–243ZG |
| Part IXB | Co-operative Societies (**97th Amendment, 2011**) | 243ZH–243ZT |
| Part X | Scheduled and Tribal Areas | 244–244A |
| Part XI | Relations between the Union and the States — legislative (**245–255**) and administrative (**256–263**) | 245–263 |
| Part XII | Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits | 264–300A |
| Part XIII | **Trade, Commerce and Intercourse** within India (inspired by **Australia**) | 301–307 |
| Part XIV | Services under the Union and the States | 308–323 |
| Part XIVA | Tribunals (**42nd Amendment, 1976**) | 323A–323B |
| Part XV | Elections (Election Commission) | 324–329A |
| Part XVI | Special provisions for certain classes (SC, ST, Anglo-Indians) | 330–342 |
| Part XVII | Official Language | 343–351 |
| Part XVIII | Emergency Provisions | 352–360 |
| Part XIX | Miscellaneous (protection of President and Governors) | 361–367 |
| Part XX | Amendment of the Constitution | 368 |
| Part XXI | Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions | 369–392 |
| Part XXII | Short title, Commencement, Authoritative text in Hindi and Repeals | 393–395 |

- Parts **added later**: **IVA**, **IXA**, **IXB** and **XIVA** (Part IX was re-used for Panchayats). That takes 22 Parts to **25**.

### Andhra Pradesh in Part XXI
- **Article 371D** — special provisions for **Andhra Pradesh**: equitable opportunities in **public employment and education** for people of different parts of the state (local cadres, Administrative Tribunal); inserted by the **32nd Amendment Act, 1973**; after **2014** it applies to both **Andhra Pradesh and Telangana**.
- **Article 371E** — **Parliament** may provide for a **Central University in Andhra Pradesh** (also **32nd Amendment**).

### The 12 Schedules
| Schedule | Subject | Articles |
|---|---|---|
| **First Schedule** | Names of **States and Union Territories** and their territories | 1 and 4 |
| **Second Schedule** | **Salaries**, allowances of President, Governors, Speakers, judges, **CAG** | 59, 65, 75, 97, 125, 148, 158, 164, 186, 221 |
| **Third Schedule** | Forms of **oaths and affirmations** | 75, 84, 99, 124, 148, 164, 188, 219 |
| **Fourth Schedule** | Allocation of **Rajya Sabha** seats to states and UTs | 4 and 80 |
| **Fifth Schedule** | Administration of **Scheduled Areas** and Scheduled Tribes | 244(1) |
| **Sixth Schedule** | **Tribal Areas** of **Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram** | 244(2) and 275(1) |
| **Seventh Schedule** | **Union, State and Concurrent Lists** | 246 |
| **Eighth Schedule** | **22 languages** (originally **14**) | 344 and 351 |
| **Ninth Schedule** | Laws (mostly **land reforms**) shielded from challenge on FR grounds | 31B |
| **Tenth Schedule** | **Anti-defection** | 102 and 191 |
| **Eleventh Schedule** | **29** subjects of **Panchayats** | 243G |
| **Twelfth Schedule** | **18** subjects of **Municipalities** | 243W |

### How the Schedules grew
- The idea of Schedules came from the **GoI Act 1935**, which had **10** Schedules. They keep detail out of the main text and make amendment easier.
- **Ninth** — added by the **1st Amendment Act, 1951**. In **I.R. Coelho (2007)** the Supreme Court held that laws placed in it **after 24 April 1973** can be reviewed if they violate the **basic structure**.
- **Tenth** — **52nd Amendment Act, 1985**. **Eleventh** — **73rd (1992)**; **Twelfth** — **74th (1992)**.

## Don't confuse
- **Fifth Schedule = Scheduled Areas** in most states; **Sixth Schedule = Tribal Areas** of the four north-eastern states.
- **Part XIII (trade and commerce) is from Australia** — like the Concurrent List.
- **Ninth Schedule came by the 1st Amendment**, not a "9th Amendment" (the source PDF says 9th — a slip).

**TL;DR**
- Parts I–XXII + IVA, IXA, IXB, XIVA = 25; Part VII repealed in 1956.
- XI Union-State relations (245–263); XII finance (264–300A); XIII trade (301–307); XV elections (324–329A); XVII language (343–351); XX amendment (368).
- Article 371D (32nd Amendment 1973) protects local cadres in Andhra Pradesh; 371E – Central University.
- Schedules: 1 States/UTs; 2 salaries; 3 oaths; 4 Rajya Sabha; 5 Scheduled Areas; 6 NE tribal areas; 7 lists; 8 languages; 9 Art 31B; 10 anti-defection; 11 Panchayats (29); 12 Municipalities (18).
keyPoints: Part VII (Part B states) was repealed by the 7th Amendment (1956); Part VIII covers Union Territories (239-242).
Part XIII (Trade, Commerce and Intercourse, Articles 301-307) is inspired by the Australian Constitution.

Part XII = Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits (264-300A); Part XV = Elections (324-329A); Part XVII = Official Language (343-351); Part XXI = Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (369-392).
Article 371D (32nd Amendment 1973) gives Andhra Pradesh equitable opportunities in public employment and education; Article 371E provides for a Central University in Andhra Pradesh.
Second Schedule = salaries; Third = oaths; Fourth = Rajya Sabha seats (Articles 4 and 80); Sixth = tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Tenth Schedule rests on Articles 102 and 191; Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects (243G); Twelfth lists 18 subjects (243W).
Eighth Schedule began with 14 languages and now has 22; I.R. Coelho (2007): Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 are open to basic-structure review.

items.title: For Mains — Salient Features & the Preamble
items.body:
## Why Mains asks this (Paper-III, Polity & Governance)

This theme (clauses M3-1 and M3-15a) is examined as **analysis of design choices**, not fact-recall. The two hot sub-themes are (a) the Preamble as the Constitution's philosophy and whether it binds, and (b) the quasi-federal balance.

| Dimension | Points to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Features** | Lengthiest written; quasi-federal (Art 1 'Union of States'); parliamentary but not sovereign; blend of rigidity/flexibility (Art 368); single citizenship; integrated judiciary |
| **Significance of Preamble** | Declares source, nature, objectives, date; aid to interpretation; 'identity card' / 'soul' of the Constitution |
| **Judicial evolution** | Berubari (1960) not part → Kesavananda (1973) part & amendable within basic structure → LIC (1995) integral but non-justiciable |
| **Criticism / tension** | 'Secular/Socialist' added by 42nd Amendment (1976) debated; quasi-federal centralisation vs. state autonomy; welfare promise vs. non-justiciable DPSP |
| **Way forward** | Cooperative federalism (GST Council, Inter-State Council); 'living constitution' reading |

**Data / authorities to quote:** K.M. Munshi ('horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'); Thakur Das Bhargava ('soul of the Constitution'); N.A. Palkhivala ('identity card of the Constitution'); Kesavananda Bharati (1973), S.R. Bommai (1994, secularism as basic structure), Berubari (1960), LIC (1995); K.C. Wheare's 'quasi-federation'; 106th Amendment (2023) as proof of a living document.

**AP angle:** Article 1's 'Union of States' and the centre's reorganisation power under Article 3 are exactly what enabled the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** (bifurcation) — a live illustration that states have no indestructible territory and that federalism in India is centre-tilted.

**Use in answers:** open an answer on the Preamble by quoting Palkhivala's 'identity card'; use the three-case ladder (Berubari → Kesavananda → LIC) as a crisp timeline; for federalism, cite S.R. Bommai and the Art 1/Art 3 point with the AP-2014 example; close by framing the Constitution as a 'living document' validated by 106 amendments. A simple Preamble-components diagram (source · nature · objectives · date) adds structure.
keyPoints: Lead Preamble answers with its four components and the 'soul/identity card' quotations.
Use the Berubari (1960) → Kesavananda (1973) → LIC (1995) ladder for the 'is it a part?' question.
Argue quasi-federalism via Art 1 'Union of States', centre-tilt features, and S.R. Bommai (1994).
Note the 42nd Amendment (1976) debate over adding Socialist/Secular; secularism is basic structure.
AP angle: Art 1/Art 3 reorganisation power underpins the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 (bifurcation).
Frame the Constitution as a living document — 106 amendments to date (106th, 2023).
items.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India; Constituent Assembly Debates
